REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] These are the reasons for decision in the refugee protection claims made by XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, who claim to be citizens of Djibouti. They are claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
Summary of allegations - Marriage on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1992, according to the document written in Somali

[2] XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Djibouti and no other country. She married XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1990, and during that relationship, she had XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX children: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX. She is a member of the Yonis Moussa tribe and has been a member of the Mouvement pour le renouveau démocratique et le développement (MRD) [movement for democratic renewal and development] since 2013.

[3] The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, with her husband and her daughter XXXX. Her husband left Canada for Ethiopia on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, to join the other XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX children and their grandmother, who are currently there.

[4] The claimant's problems with the Djiboutian authorities began on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015, when she was helping to prepare food for a traditional celebration of her Yonis Moussa tribe in Bouldhoqo. Armed police officers showed up at the group's gathering place at around 4:00 a.m. and opened fire on the civilians, killing and wounding many of them. Fortunately, she was able to get away without being hurt.

[5] That afternoon, a police officer came to the claimant's home and served her with a summons to appear at the central police station in Djibouti. However, even before she could report to the police station, two police officers came to her home at 9:00 a.m. on XXXX XXXX to arrest her and took her to the police station by force.

[6] The claimant was detained there for two days on the grounds that she had attended the celebration of her Yonis Moussa tribe on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015. During her detention, she was mistreated, slapped several times while she was being interrogated, and held in a dirty cell. After she was released, she went to the XXXX medical centre for treatment.

[7] In XXXX 2017, while the claimant was attending a meeting of the MRD to organize an anti-government protest, an infiltrator must have reported them and she received another summons to appear at the police station in the fifth arrondissement the next day. When the police officer gave her the summons, he shoved her for no reason. After the officer left, given his behaviour, she left her home and went into hiding at her friend XXXX home.

[8] The claimant was found on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, taken to the police station by force, and once again arbitrarily detained. During her second detention, she was slapped repeatedly on her right ear. The police accused her of being a member of the Yonis Moussa tribe and of working for XXXX XXXX. She was not released until the following day, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. She went to the medical centre for a second time to receive care for her ear. That is when she decided to leave the country. She helped her mother and her children leave for Ethiopia; her daughter XXXX remained with her in Djibouti.

[9] In the meantime, the claimant's younger sister XXXX became ill: she had problems with her XXXX and was losing blood. As she is the oldest sibling, she accompanied her to Dubai for treatment on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. She ran into her cousin XXXX XXXX in a shopping centre there. She told him about her problems. XXXX XXXX is a fierce opponent of the government of Djibouti. He had problems with the authorities and was accused of taking part in a corruption scheme in Djibouti. He is now in exile in Dubai.

[10] When the claimant returned to Djibouti with her younger sister on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, she was arrested for the third time at the airport and placed in a room to be questioned about why she had met with XXXX XXXX XXXX during her stay in Dubai. She was then taken to a police station, where she once again experienced physical and mental abuse that was far worse than the previous times. She was slapped, beaten and stripped naked in a dirty cell full of urine and excrement. She was told that this was her last chance and that she had to end her political activities. A relative took her to a military hospital for treatment.

[11] The claimant fears returning to Djibouti because of her problems and her political involvement with the MRD party, because of her cousin who is a fierce opponent of the government, and because she is a member of the Yonis Moussa tribe.

[12] These, in essence, are the claimants' reasons for claiming refugee protection in Canada.

[15] Section 106 of the IRPA and rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules1 state that the onus is on the claimant to produce acceptable documentation establishing identity. Where the claimant is unable to do so, the panel must take into account whether the claimant has provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or has taken reasonable steps to obtain it.2

[16] XXXX XXXX XXXX was allegedly born on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, in Djibouti and is a citizen of no other country. She supposedly married XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1990. During that relationship, they allegedly had XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX children: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX, who is an associate claimant in this refugee protection claim. In this case, all of the family members are allegedly citizens of Djibouti. The claimants provided copies of their passports and other documents from Djibouti in support of their refugee protection claims in Canada.3

[17] The Minister's evidence in this case shows that the claimants gave inconsistent and contradictory statements regarding their identities. In addition, the written account provided with their refugee protection claims differs from the account that was submitted in other circumstances, in support of an application for permanent residence in Canada.

[18] An application for permanent residence (APR) signed on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, was submitted under the Private Sponsorship of Refugees program (the PSR program). The PSR program enables the Government of Canada to resettle refugees and persons in refugee-like situations. The claimants were supported in their immigration to Canada by a sponsorship agreement holder, namely the XXXX XXXX of Rupert's Land,4 in Winnipeg, Manitoba.

[19] According to the APR filed in 2009, XXXX XXXX XXXX, born in Mogadishu on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and married to XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Somalia and had been living in Yemen since XXXX 2006. Her associated daughter in this case, XXXX XXXX XXXX, born on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Mogadishu, is also allegedly a citizen of Somalia and was also living in Yemen with her family.

[20] The APR was processed and refused by the Canadian visa office in Abu Dhabi. The claimants omitted this information from their refugee protection claims.

[21] The panel also notes that the documentation provided for the APR states that the claimant's name is XXXX XXXX XXXX and that she is a citizen of Somalia, not XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Djibouti. In the APR and the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), her father's last name is XXXX XXXXnot XXXX.

[22] Her daughter, the associate claimant, is identified as XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Somalia, in the APR, whereas her identity in her refugee protection claim is XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Djibouti. The last name of all of the claimant's children is XXXX, not XXXX, which is the last name provided in the documentation submitted under the Djiboutian citizenship.

[27] When a refugee protection claimant swears to the truth of certain facts, this creates a presumption that those facts are true unless there is a valid reason to doubt their truthfulness.5 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.6 Through her testimony, the claimant gave the panel every reason to doubt the truthfulness of her allegations, in particular their Djiboutian identities.

[28] In fact, the claimant's oral testimony was far from candid. She stated that she had never used any other first or last name. However, her last name is XXXX according to the APR, and in the documents from Djibouti, the last name declared for the purposes of her refugee protection claim is XXXX, while in both cases, her father's name is XXXX.

[29] The claimant's daughter's last name in the APR is XXXX, which is also her father's last name and the last name of the other children in the family, whereas she used her first name, XXXX, as a last name in her claim for refugee protection against Djibouti.

[30] In this case, the use of new last names and new information under a new citizenship after failing to mention that an application for residence in Canada had been refused leads the panel to conclude that the documents issued in Djibouti are documents of convenience, or even fraudulent.

argument_evidence.context_text: Section 106 of the IRPA makes it clear that identity issues go to the credibility of a claimant.
The panel is of the view that there is sufficient evidence to show that the claimants' identities have not been established.

[31] The panel is of the opinion that the presentation of such information supported by documents sworn under oath in an effort to mislead the panel is sufficient in itself to wholly destroy their credibility.
[32] In sum, after considering and weighing all of the evidence in this case, the panel finds that the claimants are neither credible nor trustworthy.

[33] In light of the above analysis, and based on the panel's overall assessment of this case, the claimants have failed to establish their identities by means of credible and trustworthy evidence, in particular with respect to their citizenship.

The panel is of the view that there is sufficient evidence to show that the claimants' identities have not been established. Section 106 of the IRPA makes it clear that identity issues go to the credibility of a claimant.7

[32] In sum, after considering and weighing all of the evidence in this case, the panel finds that the claimants are neither credible nor trustworthy. The claimant attempted to put forward "clearly fraudulent" allegations in order to obtain refugee protection in Canada as a citizen of Djibouti. Even then, her oral testimony revealed that she had fabricated a story about Djibouti based on newspaper articles; when she was questioned, it eventually came out that the cousin she refers to in her written account is not a relative.
CONCLUSION

[33] In light of the above analysis, and based on the panel's overall assessment of this case, the claimants have failed to establish their identities by means of credible and trustworthy evidence, in particular with respect to their citizenship.

[34] XXXX XXXX XXXX and her daughter XXXX are neither "Convention refugees" within the meaning of section 96, nor "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

[28] In fact, the claimant's oral testimony was far from candid. She stated that she had never used any other first or last name. However, her last name is XXXX according to the APR, and in the documents from Djibouti, the last name declared for the purposes of her refugee protection claim is XXXX, while in both cases, her father's name is XXXX.

[29] The claimant's daughter's last name in the APR is XXXX, which is also her father's last name and the last name of the other children in the family, whereas she used her first name, XXXX, as a last name in her claim for refugee protection against Djibouti.

[30] In this case, the use of new last names and new information under a new citizenship after failing to mention that an application for residence in Canada had been refused leads the panel to conclude that the documents issued in Djibouti are documents of convenience, or even fraudulent.

[31] The panel is of the opinion that the presentation of such information supported by documents sworn under oath in an effort to mislead the panel is sufficient in itself to wholly destroy their credibility. The panel is of the view that there is sufficient evidence to show that the claimants' identities have not been established. Section 106 of the IRPA makes it clear that identity issues go to the credibility of a claimant.7

[32] In sum, after considering and weighing all of the evidence in this case, the panel finds that the claimants are neither credible nor trustworthy. The claimant attempted to put forward "clearly fraudulent" allegations in order to obtain refugee protection in Canada as a citizen of Djibouti. Even then, her oral testimony revealed that she had fabricated a story about Djibouti based on newspaper articles; when she was questioned, it eventually came out that the cousin she refers to in her written account is not a relative.
CONCLUSION

[33] In light of the above analysis, and based on the panel's overall assessment of this case, the claimants have failed to establish their identities by means of credible and trustworthy evidence, in particular with respect to their citizenship.

[34] XXXX XXXX XXXX and her daughter XXXX are neither "Convention refugees" within the meaning of section 96, nor "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] These are the reasons for decision in the refugee protection claims made by XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, who claim to be citizens of Djibouti. They are claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
Summary of allegations - Marriage on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1992, according to the document written in Somali

[2] XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Djibouti and no other country. She married XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1990, and during that relationship, she had XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX children: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX. She is a member of the Yonis Moussa tribe and has been a member of the Mouvement pour le renouveau démocratique et le développement (MRD) [movement for democratic renewal and development] since 2013.

[3] The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, with her husband and her daughter XXXX. Her husband left Canada for Ethiopia on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, to join the other XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX children and their grandmother, who are currently there.

[4] The claimant's problems with the Djiboutian authorities began on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015, when she was helping to prepare food for a traditional celebration of her Yonis Moussa tribe in Bouldhoqo. Armed police officers showed up at the group's gathering place at around 4:00 a.m. and opened fire on the civilians, killing and wounding many of them. Fortunately, she was able to get away without being hurt.

[5] That afternoon, a police officer came to the claimant's home and served her with a summons to appear at the central police station in Djibouti. However, even before she could report to the police station, two police officers came to her home at 9:00 a.m. on XXXX XXXX to arrest her and took her to the police station by force.

[6] The claimant was detained there for two days on the grounds that she had attended the celebration of her Yonis Moussa tribe on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015. During her detention, she was mistreated, slapped several times while she was being interrogated, and held in a dirty cell. After she was released, she went to the XXXX medical centre for treatment.

[7] In XXXX 2017, while the claimant was attending a meeting of the MRD to organize an anti-government protest, an infiltrator must have reported them and she received another summons to appear at the police station in the fifth arrondissement the next day. When the police officer gave her the summons, he shoved her for no reason. After the officer left, given his behaviour, she left her home and went into hiding at her friend XXXX home.

[8] The claimant was found on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, taken to the police station by force, and once again arbitrarily detained. During her second detention, she was slapped repeatedly on her right ear. The police accused her of being a member of the Yonis Moussa tribe and of working for XXXX XXXX. She was not released until the following day, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. She went to the medical centre for a second time to receive care for her ear. That is when she decided to leave the country. She helped her mother and her children leave for Ethiopia; her daughter XXXX remained with her in Djibouti.

[9] In the meantime, the claimant's younger sister XXXX became ill: she had problems with her XXXX and was losing blood. As she is the oldest sibling, she accompanied her to Dubai for treatment on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017. She ran into her cousin XXXX XXXX in a shopping centre there. She told him about her problems. XXXX XXXX is a fierce opponent of the government of Djibouti. He had problems with the authorities and was accused of taking part in a corruption scheme in Djibouti. He is now in exile in Dubai.

[10] When the claimant returned to Djibouti with her younger sister on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, she was arrested for the third time at the airport and placed in a room to be questioned about why she had met with XXXX XXXX XXXX during her stay in Dubai. She was then taken to a police station, where she once again experienced physical and mental abuse that was far worse than the previous times. She was slapped, beaten and stripped naked in a dirty cell full of urine and excrement. She was told that this was her last chance and that she had to end her political activities. A relative took her to a military hospital for treatment.

[11] The claimant fears returning to Djibouti because of her problems and her political involvement with the MRD party, because of her cousin who is a fierce opponent of the government, and because she is a member of the Yonis Moussa tribe.

[12] These, in essence, are the claimants' reasons for claiming refugee protection in Canada.
DETERMINATION

[13] The determinative issues in this case are identity and the credibility of the facts in support of the refugee protection claims. "Identity" means that it is expected that claimants can be identified by their first and last names, date and place of birth, as well as a country of citizenship.

[14] For the reasons that follow, the panel concludes that the claimants have not satisfactorily established their identities. Furthermore, after analyzing all the evidence in this case, the panel concludes that these refugee protection claims are manifestly unfounded.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[15] Section 106 of the IRPA and rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules1 state that the onus is on the claimant to produce acceptable documentation establishing identity. Where the claimant is unable to do so, the panel must take into account whether the claimant has provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or has taken reasonable steps to obtain it.2

[16] XXXX XXXX XXXX was allegedly born on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, in Djibouti and is a citizen of no other country. She supposedly married XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1990. During that relationship, they allegedly had XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX children: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX, who is an associate claimant in this refugee protection claim. In this case, all of the family members are allegedly citizens of Djibouti. The claimants provided copies of their passports and other documents from Djibouti in support of their refugee protection claims in Canada.3

[17] The Minister's evidence in this case shows that the claimants gave inconsistent and contradictory statements regarding their identities. In addition, the written account provided with their refugee protection claims differs from the account that was submitted in other circumstances, in support of an application for permanent residence in Canada.

[18] An application for permanent residence (APR) signed on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, was submitted under the Private Sponsorship of Refugees program (the PSR program). The PSR program enables the Government of Canada to resettle refugees and persons in refugee-like situations. The claimants were supported in their immigration to Canada by a sponsorship agreement holder, namely the XXXX XXXX of Rupert's Land,4 in Winnipeg, Manitoba.

[19] According to the APR filed in 2009, XXXX XXXX XXXX, born in Mogadishu on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and married to XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Somalia and had been living in Yemen since XXXX 2006. Her associated daughter in this case, XXXX XXXX XXXX, born on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Mogadishu, is also allegedly a citizen of Somalia and was also living in Yemen with her family.
[20] The APR was processed and refused by the Canadian visa office in Abu Dhabi. The claimants omitted this information from their refugee protection claims.

[21] The panel also notes that the documentation provided for the APR states that the claimant's name is XXXX XXXX XXXX and that she is a citizen of Somalia, not XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Djibouti. In the APR and the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), her father's last name is XXXX XXXXnot XXXX.

[22] Her daughter, the associate claimant, is identified as XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Somalia, in the APR, whereas her identity in her refugee protection claim is XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Djibouti. The last name of all of the claimant's children is XXXX, not XXXX, which is the last name provided in the documentation submitted under the Djiboutian citizenship.

[23] In addition, the evidence filed as M-1, at pages 21 to 26, indicates that the APR submitted in 2010 refers to allegations of persecution in Somalia by reason of their ethnicity, and that in Yemen, although they were refugees in that country, they were at risk of being deported to Somalia. This does not reflect the story provided in the written account attached to the BOC Form.

[24] When asked to explain this change of citizenship, from Somalian in 2009 to Djiboutian in her refugee protection claim, XXXX XXXX XXXX or XXXX categorically denied that she had tried to obtain permanent residence in Canada with the assistance of the XXXX XXXX of Rupert's Land in Winnipeg, Manitoba, and stated that she had never been to Yemen.

[25] When the claimant was confronted with the information in the Minister's evidence and her APR file, which includes photographs of each family member, she continued to deny it, then changed her testimony and stated that her husband had submitted this file without consulting her. In the panel's opinion, this does not explain the Djiboutian citizenship put forward in her refugee protection claim, whereas they were citizens of Somalia according to the APR filed in 2009, sponsored by a Canadian organization in Manitoba.

[26] In addition, when the claimant was questioned, she was unable to provide a credible explanation about what had prompted her husband to submit a complete file for the family for sponsorship by the XXXX XXXX of Rupert's Land in Winnipeg, Manitoba. She also did not try to correct her last name so that it would match the one she had provided in her claim for refugee protection against Djibouti.

[27] When a refugee protection claimant swears to the truth of certain facts, this creates a presumption that those facts are true unless there is a valid reason to doubt their truthfulness.5 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.6 Through her testimony, the claimant gave the panel every reason to doubt the truthfulness of her allegations, in particular their Djiboutian identities.

[28] In fact, the claimant's oral testimony was far from candid. She stated that she had never used any other first or last name. However, her last name is XXXX according to the APR, and in the documents from Djibouti, the last name declared for the purposes of her refugee protection claim is XXXX, while in both cases, her father's name is XXXX.

[29] The claimant's daughter's last name in the APR is XXXX, which is also her father's last name and the last name of the other children in the family, whereas she used her first name, XXXX, as a last name in her claim for refugee protection against Djibouti.

[30] In this case, the use of new last names and new information under a new citizenship after failing to mention that an application for residence in Canada had been refused leads the panel to conclude that the documents issued in Djibouti are documents of convenience, or even fraudulent.

[31] The panel is of the opinion that the presentation of such information supported by documents sworn under oath in an effort to mislead the panel is sufficient in itself to wholly destroy their credibility. The panel is of the view that there is sufficient evidence to show that the claimants' identities have not been established. Section 106 of the IRPA makes it clear that identity issues go to the credibility of a claimant.7

[32] In sum, after considering and weighing all of the evidence in this case, the panel finds that the claimants are neither credible nor trustworthy. The claimant attempted to put forward "clearly fraudulent" allegations in order to obtain refugee protection in Canada as a citizen of Djibouti. Even then, her oral testimony revealed that she had fabricated a story about Djibouti based on newspaper articles; when she was questioned, it eventually came out that the cousin she refers to in her written account is not a relative.
CONCLUSION

[33] In light of the above analysis, and based on the panel's overall assessment of this case, the claimants have failed to establish their identities by means of credible and trustworthy evidence, in particular with respect to their citizenship.
[34] XXXX XXXX XXXX and her daughter XXXX are neither "Convention refugees" within the meaning of section 96, nor "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

[35] For these reasons, the panel rejects the claims made by the individuals using the names below:
XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Djibouti, or
XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Somalia
and
XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Djibouti, or
XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Somalia

[36] In addition, based on its overall assessment of the case, the panel further concludes that these refugee protection claims are clearly fraudulent and therefore manifestly unfounded.
